abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Anti–B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR T)-cell therapy has achieved remarkable success in the treatment of multiple myeloma (MM). Although coagulation disorders and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) have been reported frequently during CAR T-cell therapy, little research has been conducted that focuses on MM patients diagnosed with DIC before CAR T-cell infusion. In this study, we reported on two patients with MM and one patient with primary plasma cell leukemia, all of whom were diagnosed with DIC before infusion with LCAR-B38M, and discussed the management and relationship between cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and DIC. After infusion of CAR T cells, all three patients experienced CRS and aggravated DIC, with CRS tending to precede the deterioration of DIC. Following timely and comprehensive treatment, which included anticoagulant therapy, replacement therapy, treatment for CRS and supportive treatment, all patients were restored to a normal coagulation profile, with two patients achieving complete response and one stable disease. Our study shows that LCAR-B38M can be administered to patients with MM and coagulopathy or DIC and managed appropriately.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a plasma cell tumor and the second most common hematological malignancy [18]. Primary plasma cell leukemia (PCL) is a rare and aggressive type of MM that usually has a worse prognosis [7]. New drugs introduced for treatment of MM have improved the prognosis of patients, and include proteasome inhibitors (e.g., carfilzomib, ixazomib), immunomodulatory drug (e.g., pomalidomide), monoclonal antibodies (e.g., daratumumab, elotuzumab), and exportin 1 (XPO1) inhibitors (e.g., selinexor). However, even after such treatments most patients relapse and often develop drug resistance [30, 38]. Therefore, it is important that novel and more effective treatment options are developed for MM patients.

Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR T)-cell therapy, an adoptive immunotherapy that introduces tumor-targeted receptors into T cells via viral transduction [4, 33], has proved successful in the treatment of several hematological malignancies. B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA), a surface protein widely expressed in malignant plasma cells [34] that provides anti-apoptotic signaling for tumor cells [26], has become an established target for MM therapy. LCAR-B38M is a CAR T cell that targets two BCMA epitopes to confer avidity [35]. We previously conducted a phase 1, single-arm, open-label trial of LCAR-B38M in patients with relapsed/refractory MM (LEGEND-2, NCT03090659) and found that LCAR-B38M demonstrated a favorable efficacy (overall response rate: 87.8%; 5-year overall survival: 49.1%) and safety profile in these patients [42, 47, 48].

Despite the powerful anti-tumor effects of CAR T-cell therapy, adverse events remain a challenge [43]. Cytokine release syndrome (CRS), a systemic inflammatory response caused by cytokines released by CAR T cells and other immune cells (such as monocytes/macrophages), is the most common adverse event during CAR T-cell therapy [5, 31], and graded using consensus criteria of the American Society for Transplantation and Cell Therapy (Table S1) [19]. Coagulation disorders are also observed after CAR T-cell therapy, with some patients even progressing to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) [17, 40]. Our previous research showed occurrence rates of coagulation disorders and DIC in patients receiving LCAR-B38M infusion of 49 and 29%, respectively, with severity of coagulation disorders related to the extent of CRS, and DIC being more common in patients with severe CRS [23].

Patients with MM tend to have coagulation disorders, such as reduced platelet level, prolonged prothrombin time (PT)/activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), and elevated levels of tissue factor (TF), factor VII, D-Dimer, and fibrin monomer (FM) [9, 11, 22], which put them at an increased risk of bleeding and thromboembolism. Geng et al. [11] reported that 43.5% of newly diagnosed MM patients had prolonged PT or APTT. Although coagulation disorders and DIC have been reported frequently during CAR T-cell therapy, little research has focused on MM patients diagnosed with DIC before CAR T-cell infusion. At present, inclusion and exclusion criteria of many clinical trials have limited some indicators of coagulation function. Thus, it remains unclear whether CAR T-cell therapy can be safely administered to patients with a history of DIC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Our study retrospectively analyzed three patients (two with MM and one with PCL) diagnosed with DIC before infusion of LCAR-B38M. These patients were assessed using three DIC scoring systems—Chinese DIC scoring system (CDSS) [24, 39], Japanese Ministry of Health and Welfare (JMHW) [2, 24], and International Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis (ISTH) [2, 24, 36], (Table S2)—to review their characteristics during infusion period and provide information from clinical experience of using CAR T-cell therapy in MM patients with DIC. This study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Independent Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University (reference number: 2016002). We confirm that we have obtained the participation informed consent and publication informed consent from all patients.

sec.title: Case 1
sec.p: A 60-year-old male was diagnosed as having had MM (immunoglobulin [Ig]A-κ type, Durie/Salmon system [DS] stage IIB, International Staging System [ISS] stage III) for 2 years. The patient had previously received 12 cycles of chemotherapy consisting of PAD (bortezomib, adriamycin, dexamethasone) × 3 cycles, RVCD (lenalidomide, bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone) × 2 cycles, with the rest of the treatment regimen unknown, and sequential oral thalidomide or lenalidomide as maintenance therapy. The patient was enrolled into the LCAR-B38M CAR T-cell therapy clinical trial. At that time, his serum IgA was 768 mg/dL and 50.5% of the bone marrow consisted of myeloma cells. Comprehensive assessment of coagulation revealed that the patient had DIC on day -6 before LCAR-B38M infusion (CDSS 6 points, JMHW 3 points, ISTH 5 points). Lymphodepletion was performed with three doses of cyclophosphamide (CTX) 300 mg/m2 on days −5, −4, −3, and he was infused with a total of 2 × 106/kg LCAR-B38M CAR T cells on days 0, 2, and 6 (20%, 30%, 50% of the total dose, respectively). On day 9, the patient developed fever with a maximum temperature of 39.1 ℃. Physical examination showed symmetrical and sunken edema on both lower limbs. Laboratory results showed liver and kidney function were normal, levels of human interleukin-2 receptor (hIL-2R), hIL-6, hIL-8, hIL-10, and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) were all above the upper limits of normal (hIL-10 was 40-fold higher than baseline level), and that he had grade 1 CRS (Fig. 1). However, because the patient had a history of lung infections, the possibility of an infection could not be ruled out. Physical cooling and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory and anti-infection drugs lowered his temperature. Edema was related to hypoproteinemia and treated using nutritional support, diuresis, and intermittent fresh frozen plasma transfusion. On day 11, the patient’s temperature increased again, up to 39.6 °C, blood pressure fluctuated at 90–110/60–80 mmHg, and bleeding points were seen on both lower limbs. His coagulation profile showed marked prolongation of PT and APTT (Table 1), and routine bloodwork showed reduced platelet count (14 × 109/L), reduced red blood cell count (1.89 × 1012/L), reduced white blood cell count (1.90 × 109/L), and a markedly elevated aspartate transaminase level (254 IU/L), suggesting progression of DIC (CDSS 7 points, JMHW 5 points, ISTH 7 points) and abnormal liver function. The next day, cytokine levels were significantly elevated, with 62-fold higher hIL-6 and 173-fold higher hIL-10 (Fig. S1), and CRS was assessed as grade 2 (Fig. 1). Consequently, he was treated with tocilizumab 400 mg, low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) 4000 IU, infusions of fresh frozen plasma, red blood cells, and platelets, and treated with erythropoietin, granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF), and liver-protective therapy. On day 13, the patient’s temperature was reduced to normal, lower limb edema was significantly resolved, and DIC was relieved (CDSS 6 points, JMHW 4 points, ISTH 5 points). On day 17, the patient had a CDSS score of 3 points, a JMHW score of 3 points, and an ISTH score of 4 points, with liver function returning to normal. On day 21, the patient’s serum IgA returned to normal. He achieved a complete response (CR) with measurable residual disease (MRD) negativity that persisted for 9 months.

sec.title: Case 2
sec.p: A 44-year-old female had been diagnosed with MM (light chain-κ type, DS stage IIIA, ISS stage I) for more than 1 year. She was treated with six cycles of BCD (bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone), autologous stem cell transplantation, and two cycles of bortezomib + dexamethasone + lenalidomide. Subsequently, she was enrolled for LCAR-B38M CAR T-cellular immunotherapy. At admission, her level of free κ-chain was 482 mg/L, free λ-chain was 11.1 mg/L, and 67% of bone marrow was myeloma cells. Comprehensive assessment of coagulation revealed that the patient did not have DIC at enrolment (CDSS 2 points, JMHW 1 points, ISTH 3 points). After lymphodepletion with CTX (300 mg/m2, once a day, three times in total), the patient showed obvious bone marrow suppression combined with lung infection, and was given comprehensive anti-infective and symptomatic treatments to promote both white blood cell and red blood cell counts. After 1 month, the infection was controlled but the primary disease progressed: level of free κ-chain was 220 mg/L, free λ-chain was 8.98 mg/L, 81% of bone marrow was myeloma cells, and she had concomitant DIC (CDSS 6 points, JMHW 4 points, ISTH 5 points). The patient was re-enrolled for CAR T therapy and lymphodepleted again (CTX 300 mg/m2, once a day, three times in total). She was infused with a total of 1.37 × 106/kg LCAR-B38M CAR T cells in three infusions on days 0, 2, and 6 (20%, 30%, 50% of the total dose, respectively). On day 4, the patient developed intermittent fever, which lasted for 10 days, with a maximum temperature of 40.2 ℃. On day 9, the patient developed fever, chest tightness, shortness of breath; the symptoms were improved after antipyretic, anti-infection treatment and low-flow oxygen inhalation. On day 12, the patient’s fever worsened, her blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg, and hIL-2R, hIL-6, hIL-10, TNF-α levels exceeded the upper limits of normal (Fig. S2). hIL-10 was eight-fold higher than baseline, and CRS was assessed as grade 2 (Fig. 2). Routine bloodwork showed reduced platelet count (16 × 109/L), reduced red blood cell count (2.19 × 1012/L), and a reduced white blood cell count (1.64 × 109/L), and DIC scoring systems suggested that DIC was persistent (CDSS 6 points, JMHW 4 points, ISTH 5 points). Consequently, she was administered tocilizumab 400 mg, fluid rehydration, LMWH 4000 IU, infusions of red blood cells and platelets, and G-CSF. On day 16, the patient’s temperature returned to normal. Her platelet level was extremely low, whereas her D-Dimer and fibrin/fibrinogen degradation product (FDP) levels were markedly elevated (CDSS 6 points, JMHW 4 points, ISTH 5 points, Table 2). LMWH and platelets transfusion were administered. On day 17, the patient developed a nosebleed after sneezing and routine bloodwork showed low levels of platelets, red blood cells, and white blood cells. Norepinephrine-infused cotton balls, platelet and red blood cell transfusion, thrombopoietin and G-CSF were given. Bleeding was controlled. On day 26, the patient developed scattered fresh bleeding points on both lower limbs, which were caused by bone marrow suppression and low platelet levels after the infusion of CAR T cells. At this point, the patient was no longer considered to be comorbid DIC (CDSS 3 points, JMHW 2 point, ISTH 4 points). Hemostasis, platelets transfusion, and thrombopoietin were given, with no fresh bleeding thereafter. On day 30, her free light chain level decreased to normal, results of blood and urine immunofixation electrophoresis were negative, and no myeloma cells were seen on bone marrow smears. Further evaluation showed that the disease reached CR with negative MRD, which lasted for 7 months before relapsing.

sec.title: Case 3
sec.p: A 55-year-old male had been diagnosed with primary PCL for 2 years. He was treated with nine cycles of ABCD (bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone, epirubicin), oral thalidomide and dexamethasone for more than one year, oral lenalidomide alone for more than 20 days, and a one-cycle combination chemotherapy including lenalidomide, interferon, prednisone, and cyclophosphamide. The patient was then enrolled for LCAR-B38M CAR T-cell therapy. At enrolment, the patient’s serum IgG was 7320 mg/dL, free κ-chain was 710 mg/L, 33% of bone marrow was myeloma cells, and flow cytometry analysis showed 30.6% abnormal plasma cells. On day -5, he had a CDSS score of 6 points, a JMHW score of 2 points, and an ISTH score of 5 points, leading to a diagnosis of DIC. He received three doses of CTX 300 mg/m2 for lymphodepletion on days −5, −4, −3, and was infused a total of 2.86 × 106/kg LCAR-B38M CAR T cells on days 0, 2 and 6 (20%, 30%, 50% of the total dose, respectively). On day 9, the patient developed fever, which lasted for 8 days, with a maximum temperature of 40.9 °C. On the same day, he developed hypotension (88/56 mmHg) and abnormal renal function while his liver function was normal. Laboratory results showed that hIL-1β, hIL-2R, hIL-6, hIL-10, and TNF-α levels exceeded the upper limits of normal, leading to a grade 2 CRS diagnosis. Antipyretic treatment and fluid rehydration support were given. On day 12, the patient developed hypoxemia (90% oxygen saturation) with significantly elevated levels of both hIL-6 (156-fold above baseline) and hIL-10 (24-fold above baseline; Fig. S3). Tocilizumab 480 mg and symptomatic therapies including fluid rehydration, anti-infection and antipyretic treatments, and low-flow oxygen inhalation were administered. Vital signs were closely monitored by cardiogram. On day 14, routine bloodwork showed that his platelet count was 8 × 109/L, white blood cell count was 0.84 × 109/L, and red blood cell count was 2.54 × 1012/L. Platelet suspension, thrombopoietin and G-CSF were administered. Two days later, the patient’s symptoms were relieved and renal function returned to normal. However, his CDSS score was 7 points, JMHW score was 4 points, ISTH score was 5 points, and DIC was aggravated (Table 3), and LMWH was administered for aggravated DIC. On day 19, the patient’s serum IgG decreased to 3860 mg/dL, free κ-chain decreased to 169 mg/L, and myeloma was evaluated as stable disease (SD). Further evaluation on day 50 showed that his serum IgG level increased to 8330 mg/dL, free κ-chain increased to 422 mg/L, and 46.12% of bone marrow was abnormal, after which he received other antimyeloma treatment.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: MM accounts for about 10% of hematological malignancies and its incidence is gradually increasing [27, 28]. Since most patients still relapse after treatment, MM is considered an incurable disease. CAR T-cell therapy has changed the treatment pattern of MM patients and significantly improved their prognosis [8]. Currently, two CAR T-cell products targeting BCMA are approved for marketing by the US Food and Drug Administration, idecabtagene vicleucel (ide-cel) and ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) [13, 37]. Berdeja et al. [3] demonstrated the efficacy of cilta-cel by reporting an overall response rate of 97%, with 67% stringent CR and a 12-month progression-free survival rate of 77%. However, CAR T-cell therapy has triggered some adverse events along with its powerful therapeutic effects. Although CRS and neurotoxicity are the most common toxic reactions [8, 35], coagulation disorder has been reported increasingly over recent years. Some patients only show abnormal coagulation parameters, whereas others may go on to develop DIC [29]. Our previous study showed that incidence of coagulation disorders after CAR T-cell therapy was 49% and incidence of DIC was 29%, coagulopathy was associated with CRS and was more common in patients with high-grade CRS [23]. Although coagulation disorders and DIC are frequently reported during CAR T-cell therapy, few studies have focused on MM patients diagnosed with DIC before CAR T-cell infusion.

In this study, we reported three patients (two with MM and one with PCL) who were diagnosed with DIC before LCAR-B38M infusion, with their DIC possibly related to progression or recurrence of the primary disease. Malignant tumor cells tend to express abnormal levels of TF, which can form a complex with factor VIIa and activate factors IX and X to initiate the coagulation pathway and produce thrombin [20]. Thrombin not only enhances the coagulation cascade reaction but also induces platelet activation and fibrin formation [1]. In addition, tumor cells may produce TNF-α and other cytokines to damage vascular endothelial cells, which increases the release of TF and von Willebrand factor (vWF), and decreases expression of thrombomodulin (TM) [1, 16, 20, 21]. All three patients also received chemotherapy and other anti-tumor cell therapy. These treatments can induce tumor cell apoptosis, releasing substances that cause coagulation disorders and exacerbating the risk of DIC [16, 20]. Moreover, chemotherapy can damage endothelial cells, increasing the risk of thrombosis through the above-mentioned pathways [20].

Since the severity of DIC in these three patients was not life-threatening before CAR T-cell infusion (just sufficient to meet diagnosis criteria), we administered CAR T-cell infusion as planned, and monitored closely with routine blood and coagulation assessment. After infusion of CAR T cells, CRS and DIC progression occurred in all three patients, but none of them developed neurotoxicity or tumor cytolysis syndrome. CRS appeared on days 9, 12 and 9, peaked on days 12, 14 and 12. In the days before or after the cytokine peak, all three patients experienced DIC progression (elevated DIC scores or significant changes in coagulation parameters; Figs. 1 and 2). This suggested that CRS may be responsible for the progression of DIC. CRS usually develops within 2 weeks of CAR T cells infusion [10, 14]. Recognition of tumor antigens activates CAR T cells, resulting in the release of cytokines such as IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α, GM-CSF, and IFN-γ and the killing of tumor cells [25]. Then, activated CAR T cells and debris from dead tumor cells further activate other immune cells, especially monocytes/macrophages, leading to release of IL-6, IL-1, IL-10, TNF-α, NO and other cytokines, which bring about a systemic inflammatory response [31, 41, 46]. IL-6 plays a significant role in CRS and CRS-related coagulation disorders. Our study showed that all three cases had a significant increase in IL-6 level at the time of CRS, with peak levels of 62-, 12-, and 156-fold higher than baseline, respectively. IL-6 activates vascular endothelial cells, and promotes expression and release of IL-6, IL-8, angiopoietin 2, monocyte chemotactic protein-1 (MCP-1), and the plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) [40, 41, 44]. These inflammatory factors induce vascular endothelial cells to release of TF and vWF, and disrupt the tight junctions between vascular endothelial cells, leading to increased vascular permeability and leakage [6, 12, 15, 17]. High concentrations of cytokines may lead to hepatocellular damage, not only affecting the synthesis of some coagulation proteins, but also inhibiting ADAMTS13 (an enzyme that cleaves vWF) thereby leading to elevated vWF levels and promoting platelet adhesion and aggregation [6, 45]. In addition, P-selectin may also be involved in the development of DIC [32].

After progression of DIC, we managed treatment of the three patients using four methods: (1) Anticoagulant therapy. All patients were administered LMWH 4000 IU per day until DIC score returned to within normal limits. (2) Replacement therapy. One patient had significantly prolonged PT/APTT and was administered fresh frozen plasma. All patients presented with reduced platelets and were transfused with platelets to maintain platelet level above 20 × 109/L (when platelets were less than 10 × 109/L, thrombopoietin was added). All patients had lowered red and white blood cell counts, and were treated with red blood cell suspension and G-CSF. (3) Treatment for CRS. All three patients developed grade 2 CRS and were treated with the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab. (4) Supportive treatment, such as liver-protective treatment. Ultimately, two patients achieved CR and one patient achieved SD.

In conclusion, we demonstrated that the safety of CAR T-cell therapy could be ensured by close observation and comprehensive treatment despite the presence of DIC before the infusion of CAR T-cells. Our study provided experience of clinical practice in the use of CAR T-cell therapy in MM patients with coagulopathy and even DIC.
